reference.source: Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology / Cornea by Krachmer
clinicalPearls: A spectrum of disorders caused by an abnormal, proliferative corneal endothelium that migrates across the angle and onto the iris
Typically unilateral and affecting middle-aged women, presenting with corneal oedema, iris changes, or secondary glaucoma
The three overlapping clinical variants are essential (progressive) iris atrophy, Chandler syndrome, and Cogan-Reese (iris naevus) syndrome
Essential iris atrophy shows marked iris thinning, hole formation, corectopia (pupil displacement), and pseudopolycoria
Chandler syndrome is dominated by endothelial change and corneal oedema with relatively mild iris atrophy
Cogan-Reese syndrome features pigmented iris nodules on the abnormal endothelial-lined membrane
Specular microscopy shows characteristic ICE cells with a dark-light reversal (epithelial-like) appearance of the endothelium

Management targets the two main problems: corneal oedema (medical measures then endothelial keratoplasty) and secondary angle-closure glaucoma (medical, laser, or surgical, often with drainage devices)
reference.pathophysiology: Iridocorneal endothelial syndrome is characterised by an acquired abnormality of the corneal endothelium, whose cells take on epithelial-like proliferative and migratory behaviour. These abnormal endothelial cells and an accompanying basement-membrane-like layer proliferate across the trabecular meshwork and over the anterior iris surface. Contraction of this membrane produces peripheral anterior synechiae, angle closure, iris stretching with corectopia, iris hole formation, and, in the Cogan-Reese variant, pigmented iris nodules. Blockage of the trabecular meshwork by the membrane and synechiae raises intraocular pressure, causing secondary glaucoma, while endothelial dysfunction leads to corneal oedema. The condition is typically unilateral and slowly progressive.
additionalDifferentials: Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome and other anterior segment dysgenesis
Peripheral anterior synechiae from chronic angle-closure or uveitis
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination documenting corneal oedema, iris atrophy, corectopia, and nodules
Specular or confocal microscopy showing abnormal ICE endothelial cells
Gonioscopy to assess peripheral anterior synechiae and angle closure
Intraocular pressure measurement and glaucoma assessment with optic nerve and visual field evaluation
Anterior segment optical coherence tomography or ultrasound biomicroscopy of the angle and iris membrane
Pachymetry to assess corneal oedema and guide surgical planning
redFlags: Progressive secondary glaucoma with optic nerve damage and field loss
Corneal decompensation with worsening oedema and visual loss
Rapidly advancing iris destruction and corectopia
Features suggesting iris melanoma rather than the benign nodules of Cogan-Reese syndrome
reference.prognosis: The syndrome is slowly progressive and often difficult to control, with secondary glaucoma frequently requiring surgery and a tendency for corneal decompensation over time. Endothelial keratoplasty can restore corneal clarity, but glaucoma commonly limits the long-term visual outcome.
pitfalls: Mistaking ICE syndrome for Fuchs or posterior polymorphous dystrophy, which are usually bilateral
Underestimating the aggressive, often refractory secondary glaucoma
Confusing Cogan-Reese iris nodules with iris melanoma
Attributing unilateral corneal oedema to primary endothelial dystrophy without gonioscopy and specular microscopy
references: Cornea by Krachmer, Mannis and Holland
management: Lower intraocular pressure medically with aqueous suppressants such as topical beta-blockers, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and alpha-agonists as first-line for the secondary glaucoma
Proceed to glaucoma surgery, either trabeculectomy with an antimetabolite or a glaucoma drainage device, when medical therapy fails, as it commonly does
Treat corneal decompensation with endothelial or penetrating keratoplasty to restore clarity
Relieve symptomatic corneal oedema initially with hypertonic saline drops alongside control of intraocular pressure
Monitor with intraocular pressure, optic nerve and visual field assessment, specular or confocal microscopy and pachymetry
Refer for combined glaucoma and corneal subspecialist management given the progressive, often refractory course
